name: ALG8-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ih)

clinicalPearls: ALG8 encodes glucosyltransferase II (dolichyl-pyrophosphate Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 alpha-1,3-glucosyltransferase), which adds the second of the three terminal glucose residues to the lipid-linked oligosaccharide, immediately after the ALG6 step.

The phenotype is frequently severe and multisystem, dominated by protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminaemia, generalised oedema and ascites, and it can present antenatally as non-immune hydrops.
Hepatic involvement (hepatomegaly, hepatic fibrosis and failure) with coagulopathy and both bleeding and thrombosis risk is prominent.
Ophthalmological findings include cataract, and renal involvement and ichthyosis-like skin changes have been reported.
Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin shows a type I pattern; fibroblast lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis reveals accumulation of Glc1Man9GlcNAc2.
Milder survivors present with developmental delay and intellectual disability, with variable epilepsy.
Distinguish from ALG6-CDG (glucosyltransferase I, which adds the first glucose); the phenotypes overlap but the enzymatic block differs.
reference.pathophysiology: ALG8-CDG is an autosomal recessive type I congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by biallelic variants in ALG8, which encodes dolichyl-pyrophosphate Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 alpha-1,3-glucosyltransferase (glucosyltransferase II) in the endoplasmic reticulum. This enzyme adds the second of the three terminal glucose residues onto the mature Man9GlcNAc2 lipid-linked oligosaccharide, a step required before the glucose-trimming quality-control cycle that permits transfer of the complete Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 glycan to asparagine residues of nascent glycoproteins. Loss of activity causes accumulation of the monoglucosylated precursor and reduced N-glycosylation site occupancy, so glycoproteins governing intestinal barrier integrity, coagulation, and hepatic and ocular function become hypoglycosylated, explaining the characteristic protein-losing enteropathy, oedema, coagulopathy and hepatopathy.
additionalDifferentials: ALG6-CDG (CDG-Ic), the immediately upstream glucosyltransferase step
PMM2-CDG (CDG-Ia), the prototypic type I CDG
MPI-CDG (CDG-Ib), a hepatic-intestinal CDG that also causes protein-losing enteropathy
Primary congenital protein-losing enteropathies and intestinal lymphangiectasia
Other genetic and non-genetic causes of non-immune fetal hydrops
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing / carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (type I pattern)
CDG gene panel or exome sequencing confirming biallelic ALG8 variants
Lipid-linked oligosaccharide profiling in cultured fibroblasts
Serum albumin and faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin to document protein-losing enteropathy
Coagulation panel including antithrombin, protein C and S, and fibrinogen
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging
redFlags: Antenatal or neonatal hydrops, or refractory oedema and ascites
Severe protein-losing enteropathy with profound hypoalbuminaemia
Sepsis-like clinical decompensation in early infancy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is often poor, with high infant mortality in the severe multisystem form, whereas milder genotypes may survive with developmental delay and intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the enteropathy or hydrops as a primary gastrointestinal or cardiac disorder and missing the underlying glycosylation defect.
A normal or near-normal transferrin pattern in early neonatal life falsely reassuring the clinician.
Confusing ALG8-CDG with ALG6-CDG without enzymatic, lipid-linked oligosaccharide or genetic distinction.
Managing the oedema symptomatically without addressing the underlying protein loss and coagulopathy.
references: Standard inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Peer-reviewed reviews of congenital disorders of glycosylation
Clinical genetics and neurometabolic disease references
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; supportive management targets the protein-losing enteropathy, hepatic and coagulation complications
Manage protein-losing enteropathy with albumin replacement, nutritional support and dietetic input for hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and ascites
Correct coagulopathy and balance bleeding against thrombotic risk with replacement of deficient factors and anticoagulant proteins under haematology guidance
Monitor hepatic involvement with liver function tests and hepatology input as fibrosis progresses towards hepatic failure
Provide ophthalmology review for cataract and manage renal and ichthyosiform skin manifestations
Support development and any epilepsy in survivors with neurology and rehabilitation input
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic care with palliative support in severe infantile disease
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
